newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mobutu envoy lands in S.Africa for key Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu envoy lands in S.Africa for key Zaire talks.

text.p: Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's special envoy arrived in South Africa on Thursday ahead of crucial peace talks with rebels who have seized control of a quarter of the country.

Honore Ngbanda, who is Mobutu's security adviser and chairs the eight-member Zairean government negotiations team which includes a military expert and members of opposition parties, disembarked at Lanseria Airport outside Johannesburg.

A plane carrying representatives of rebel leader Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire was expected to land in South Africa from Goma in rebel-held eastern Zaire within hours of Ngbanda's touchdown.

Ngbanda refused to comment on the rebels' swift rejection of an offer of six ministries in a government headed by Zaire's new Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi: "I didn't come here for that. We came here to talk, and good talks for responsible men do not take place by means of press communiques but around the negotiating table."

South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad and the joint U.N. and Organisation of African Unity envoy, Mohamed Sahnoun, met in Pretoria earlier on Thursday to discuss arrangements for the talks, which were likely to be made public on Friday, the Foreign Ministry said.

Ngabanda, speaking in French, did not say when negotiations would actually begin, adding only: "I have come first of all to meet Mr Sahnoun and the South African authorities to fix the date of the official start of negotiations."

According to news reports in South Africa the two sides were expected to meet in Pretoria or Johannesburg, both in the heartlands Gauteng province, on Saturday -- but no precise date, schedule or location has been announced.

Pahad earlier told state radio South Africa had gained the impression from Kabila, who held preparatory discussions in Pretoria last month, that he was committed to democracy in the central African country.
"We've always had the feeling from the first proximity talks in South Africa that the rebels were committed to finding a peaceful solution.

"They wanted to be sure the negotiations would not take place over a protracted period...and ultimately they wanted to be sure that any negotiations must have as an objective finding the process that will lead to genuine democracy," Pahad said.
